prompt: Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: Can an 8-Person StartUp Sell to a CIO? Yes — If You Understand The Social Contract.
answer_a:
So I had a chance meeting recently with a very senior IT leader at one of the world’s largest companies.
A few months back, they’d decided on their new CRM and other business process app strategy for the next decade or so.  And it was … Salesforce again.
But this time, he wasn’t just buying from sales. He bought directly from the CEO.
I asked how that worked and what happened.
“Why did you buy direct?” I asked?
He said: “Because we wanted someone who would take our social contract seriously.”
That really stood out as a phrase.
“What do you mean by ‘social contract’,” I asked?
“You know, like the Founding Fathers signed a social compact” he replied. “They took an oath to uphold certain principles and standards when they governed America. We want vendors that will sign up to those same contracts. It’s not enough to have your logo and be certified or whatever. Those are table stakes now. But we need folks that will commit to making sure everything works right, no matter what happens.”
Wow.
This is something almost none of us think about these days. We’re all thinking about PLG (product-led growth) and AI agents and more. But there are still many customers where signing up for a serious social contract matters.
If nothing else, if you sell to enterprises, make sure you understand what that means. Make sure every stakeholder has skin in the game, and everyone knows it.
It can lead to real loyalty over decades.
And even to being able to close deals where you aren’t the only vendor. Or even the cheapest.
Sometimes, having fewer features is actually a competitive advantage in larger enterprise deals.
answer_b:
So I had lunch with one of my favorite ex-employees today, now running his own small but fast growing SaaS start-up at $1m ARR or so, and selling almost entirely to mid-market enterprises.  He’s doing well, but he can’t get any of them to buy from him.  Not even one.  Why not?
Because they are too small.  Too few folks on their team care enough about this little vendor to really sell it.
There is a social contract when you sell into big companies that many founders don’t quite understand until later:
The Enterprise Salesperson’s Job Is To Solve All Their Problems. At Least, It Should Be. So if your sales rep doesn’t seem very good, maybe just ask how she does it. And then listen carefully to her answer. She’ll likely tell you all the problems she solves for each stakeholder at the customer … and why her product solves those problems better than others do. That may sound basic, but boy, it often isn’t. In fact, most enterprise reps aren’t trained as much here as you’d think. They are often incentivized by quota attainment per se, rather than solving the prospect/customer’s problem(s). But you want someone whose job is to solve all your problems. Because there will be more and more problems to solve over time. And a great sales exec knows that every stakeholder has different needs. A VP of Marketing may need automation, and help with getting out of spam filters. A Head of IT Security needs integrations and data encryption. An admin wants ease-of-use. Etc. etc. One way to look at it is that in the early days, you have to be like a point solution. Later, you grow up and become the system of record.

So there’s been a lot of worry among VCs and public market investors that public SaaS multiples are too low.
I.e., that they’re not high enough for folks to make money investing.
This is true — from a purely financial perspective.  A $10B ARR company growing 30% at an average price-to-revenue multiple today might only trade around 8x or so.   That would be tough on your VC fund if you invested all the way back when it was worth $2B ARR.
But here’s what I think:
Public multiples aren’t really relevant to start-ups
. Why not?
First, most founders don’t care much about their “valuation” as long as they have plenty of runway (i.e., cash). And second, even with lower valuations … IPOs remain hot.
In fact, revenue has grown 27% at Adobe Sign / EchoSign since its IPO
Squarespace grew +39%
Monday.com grew 55%
ZoomInfo grew 63%
Deals like this keep happening again and again.
Why? Because growth rates stay strong,
And importantly, because the markets still love SaaS leaders that are truly dominating their space.  The ones with epic NRR and epic growth.
If you are one of those, then ignore the noise.  Ignore the fact that others may have fallen out of favor, or that multiples are down.
The best will always find a home at top prices.
answer_b:
But there are real downsides to having public company multiples as your yardstick for private valuations:
They’re not always correlated with growth rates or cash flow
– Many high-growth companies trade at lower multiples than slow-growing ones because they have less revenue and therefore less GAAP profitability. This creates an arbitrage opportunity for investors who can buy shares cheaply now and sell them later when the multiple expands as the company grows.
You’ll miss the early-stage value creation
– The biggest returns on investment often come from early rounds where you pay low prices relative to what the company will eventually be worth. Using public company multiples would make it hard to justify those investments. For example, if you invest $10 million into a startup that raises at a $150M pre-money valuation (which is common) but ends up being acquired for $1B several years down the road, you’d never get funded using public company metrics alone. It’s also important to remember that
the best startups don’t look like publicly traded companies at any given time
. They may have different business models, customer acquisition strategies, or competitive dynamics that make direct comparisons difficult. The venture industry has historically been willing to tolerate this divergence in exchange for potentially higher long-term returns, even if it means accepting higher volatility along the way. At least some of us do, anyway 😉
Ultimately, whether or not to use public company multiples depends on your specific circumstances and goals. If you’re raising money from institutional investors who expect consistent quarterly returns, following the pack might feel safer. Q:  I’m an SMB SaaS company with relatively high churn and low net retention. I’ve been growing my revenue at a good rate, but if your Net Retention Rate (NRR) is below 100% … you’ll run out of room.
You will grow faster than average for a while — because there are so many more customers you can get. But eventually, it all runs out. And then growth decelerates dramatically. It’s hard enough to hit $10m ARR with even a mediocre product. You may well be able to do better with say a 120%-130% NRR … if you have something great. Even without being truly enterprise-grade. But if your NRR is too low, you won’t really make it past that first initial phase. So what should we do?
A few thoughts:
First, don’t overindex on “churn reduction” as your top goal. That sounds easy, but it isn’t. The best way to reduce churn is to increase net negative churn. Get them spending more money, not just keeping their credit cards in their wallets. This means focusing most of your energy here after $1m-$2m ARR or so, when you have enough data to see which accounts you can upsell into. Second, stop blaming everyone else for your problems
. Your competitors often aren’t doing much better. Third, focus on increasing ACV per customer. A bit more here:
How To Increase Your Average Customer Value Per Account | SaaStr
Fourth, find some budget to invest back in sales & marketing
. At least 20% of any incremental cash flow. Yes, this means less investment in engineering. Maybe even zero new features until you’ve grown enough to justify a larger team. Fifth, push through it. In fact, once you’ve crossed Initial Traction ($5-8m+ ARR), lean in even harder now. Every dollar invested will pay off. Sixth, challenge yourself to improve NRR by X%. Not by going from -12% to +6%, but go from -11% to -9%, for example. Or maybe from 85% to 90%.

An NRR zombie is someone that has good churn and retention on paper — at least for now.
But …
They are never going to get to $100m ARR or beyond if they don’t change. And often even survive longer than that with any material growth.
Why? Because their customer count just doesn’t grow enough. Not only does this lead to very slow revenue growth (as much as 10%-20% less) due to natural account expansion … it also makes recruiting impossible. Why would anyone want to join your startup when there aren’t enough customers to hire more sales reps, support folks, success managers, etc.? The future looks too dark. So what should an NRR Zombie do?
First off, fix the root cause. That may take time. But you need to get out of the hole here:
Find a way to increase activation rates so new users start using your product earlier;
Improve the quality of leads sent to Sales; and/or
Increase the percentage of deals closed by Sales. It’s OK to lose some leads and not close every deal. It always is. At least make sure everyone knows how to maximize the chances each and every lead is closed. More on that
here
.
Do whatever it takes to improve your win rate and hit quota. Once you do, you’ll see things turn around pretty quickly, assuming you can keep the engine humming once you hit quota regularly. Your team will believe again. Second, let the rest go. Let the NRR Zombies go. Be honest who you’d be happy to let go of today. Be honest why you really can’t afford them anymore. Some won’t fit into the New World Order. And most importantly, some simply don’t care.

answer_a:
We recently deployed an AI agent that we’re genuinely excited about — it’s actually helping us generate qualified inbound leads at scale.
It works well when you train it properly:
You feed it your best content as training data
You QA every single output for accuracy
You iterate daily on edge cases
You review results constantly
But here’s what happened with our new AI SDR agent over the holidays (we learned this lesson again):
The vendor told us to just “train it” before they’d turn it live. So we did.  We trained it.  And then went off for vacation.
And then nothing worked after that.  Nothing.
The issue? When you push an AI agent into production without ongoing monitoring and maintenance,
it will break
— often in ways that aren’t immediately obvious, or even visible. This is why you need to think about AI agents like complex infrastructure deployments, not simple software purchases. Our mistake was thinking we could hand it off once we were satisfied with initial outputs and expect everything to keep working smoothly.
Why Agents Need Ongoing Human Oversight
Here are the actual issues we encountered with zero human intervention during the holiday period:
Outdated Training Data Drift
:
Our training dataset became stale while we weren’t actively checking outputs against real-time market conditions and prospect feedback patterns. Without fresh validation, responses started sounding robotic and disconnected from current market realities.
Edge Case Explosion
:
Without daily human oversight, edge case handling broke down completely. For example, the agent stopped knowing how to handle objections effectively or adapt to new sales scenarios that hadn’t been documented in historical training data.
Training Dataset Corruption
:
Someone accidentally deleted critical training materials while trying to optimize performance metrics, forcing us to rebuild entire segments of the model.
answer_b:
We trained it on our data for months. Watched it get better every week. Saw it handle edge cases we never thought about. It was genuinely good — not just good at our specific workflows, but actually useful to have around. So when I had another project that needed similar work? Easy choice. Same agent. Less training time than starting fresh. More context. Better results because it knew us already. Right decision from almost any perspective except one: maintenance.
What Actually Went Wrong (The Short Version)
Here’s what happened:
A critical bug crept into production
that should have been caught by QA
but wasn’t because nobody reviewed output anymore
It went undetected for weeks because nobody read outputs regularly
Then someone else discovered it after the damage was done
I didn’t even know until they told me. And then I looked back through our dashboards… and yeah. That’s why things slowed down. Now I’m spending time fixing issues that shouldn’t exist. This is exactly how AI agents can quietly fail you over time. They don’t break spectacularly with error messages. They just degrade gradually while you’re busy elsewhere. Or worse: they keep working, but producing subtly wrong answers that build compounding errors across your entire dataset. Why Maintenance Was So Hard To Do
This particular agent has a dashboard where everything looks fine. Outputs are green. Tasks are completed. Everything seems healthy. But here’s what actually matters:
the outputs stopped being validated against real-world expectations
. Nobody reads them daily like we used to. Nobody checks for inconsistencies between prompts and responses. Nobody verifies that the answers still make sense before moving them into production.

Dear SaaStr:  What are some strategies for handling angry customers?
Listen. If they are right, fix it — quickly.
It’s OK if your product isn’t perfect today. It will be later. But listen and address any issues that aren’t fixed yet. And do so immediately. Don’t tell them “we’ll get back to you”. Instead, just say “I can help” or “You’re right.”
Apologize
. When done authentically, this works well. Even if you didn’t do anything wrong personally.
Give them an upgrade. This doesn’t work as often as I think it should, but give away an extra seat or two if it makes their lives easier. Or even better, give them more than one thing. Give them a discount
. Sometimes, getting out of financial stress is enough. You don’t have to like it, but sometimes it really helps to reduce friction here. Offer them another chance at renewing after X months if they leave now
. This also reduces friction. The key to success with both these last two tactics is to follow through on what you promise. Otherwise, they won’t work. Don’t make excuses
. These rarely help. They almost always increase anger. Take responsibility where appropriate. Offer to talk to anyone else on the team
. This shows empathy, too, when you take ownership of an issue yourself by offering to go over someone else’s head. Be transparent
. Let them know why something happened, and how you plan to prevent it going forward. Most importantly,
listen
. Listen to see if there’s anything you could have done differently, and if there is, own up to it. Then, move on. Once you’ve listened, apologized, offered to resolve the problem, etc., then once you’ve done all those things … move on.

First, ask yourself if you can truly win them back. Sometimes it’s better just to let them go.

Let them have their data
. Don’t make it too hard for them to get out with all their data intact. This is almost always the #1 complaint when customers churn from an app.
Go visit them — IRL
. Go see your top customers IRL as often as possible. Even after they’ve signed up.
Don’t do price increases during renewals
. If you need to raise prices, raise them once a year on everyone. Not mid-contract. And be super transparent here.
Apologize
. Apologies don’t really fix anything but they help. They show empathy and understanding.
Hire a Customer Success Manager for each customer segment
. If you’re growing quickly, hire someone who specializes in retaining high-value accounts. It might not even cost that much per account.
And finally — apologize.

You’ve reached product-market fit (which you likely have if you’re at this point)

You need help with messaging consistency across channels—you might be creating great content here and there, but it doesn’t feel cohesive yet
Sales reps can’t keep up with the leads they’re generating—this is a clear sign that inbound demand exceeds your ability to handle it manually
At this stage, hiring an experienced marketing professional will pay off immediately because they’ll help scale your existing efforts without requiring you to reinvent the wheel.

The earlier you can afford to hire your first true VP Marketing (and not just an individual contributor) … the better.  It probably needs to be before $10m ARR at least.

Your First “Real” VP of Marketing is Your Bridge from Individual Contributor Marketing to True Enterprise Marketing
The thing with marketing is that it scales differently than engineering or sales. In engineering and sales, each additional team member multiplies your output by roughly x2-3x. With one great engineer, you might ship 1 feature. Add another, and you’re shipping 2 features. But with marketing—especially enterprise marketing—the impact often feels linear rather than exponential.

That person isn’t a mid-stage hire—they’re usually only ready when you’ve hit significant scaling momentum ($50+ million ARR minimum for many companies).
But if you wait too long, you’ll miss out on the opportunity to shape your brand while you still control the narrative. You’ll also risk losing deals because prospects are asking questions your product hasn’t even launched yet. The sweet spot is somewhere between $5-20 million ARR, depending on your growth rate and market complexity.

Dear SaaStr: Is it bad to leave a struggling startup?
No, not if you are leaving for something better. A chance to make even more money, or be part of an even bigger success story.
Not really.
Especially these days:
In fact, there’s one thing I can tell you that is worse than leaving a startup that isn’t working out … and that’s staying too long when your career has moved on from it.
It happens all the time with founders who struggle after an early exit, but also with execs at start-ups that aren’t growing quickly enough anymore.
I’ve watched so many folks stay in roles they are just no longer suited for. When their passion is gone, or they don’t grow into new responsibilities, etc. Sometimes, this makes sense — because there are few other options.
But often times, we see someone that could have made it as VP Eng or Chief Architect or whatever at HotCo move onto another hot start-up instead.
And then fail there, because they were always meant to be somewhere else.
If you’re doing OK (i.e., making market) where you are, it may take some pressure off.
But it’s almost never worth staying past the point you’d personally do great things.
There’s nothing wrong with moving on, especially when the company itself hasn’t been able to move on.
Go find what you’re passionate about now. And run hard towards it. It will pay dividends.
answer_b:
Dear SaaStr: Is it bad to leave a struggling startup?
It’s not that simple.
I’ve seen this question come up again and again on Quora, LinkedIn, etc.  A lot of folks have strong opinions here, especially founders. Some say you should always try harder if things aren’t working out. Others argue that everyone has limits — including their time. And then there are those who suggest you just move on … but only after helping find someone to replace yourself.
Let me share my learnings:
When I was at Adobe Sign / EchoSign,
we were acquired by Adobe for $2.6 Billion when we had 50 employees and less than $10m ARR
. It wasn’t easy getting from $0–$100M+ ARR in 5 years or so, but we made it happen. My point is it doesn’t matter what your revenue run rate is today or how many customers you have. What matters is whether you’re making meaningful progress toward your goals. If you are, stay put. You might be surprised where that journey takes you.
If you’re still early-stage (less than $20-30 million in revenue), leaving can definitely hurt more than help. The first few million dollars are brutal—getting past $1M in revenue is often the hardest part because it requires building all the infrastructure and systems that will scale with you. But once you hit initial traction ($2M-$5M in ARR), you start to build momentum. Your early wins create credibility with investors and potential hires. They make it easier to recruit top talent and secure funding for growth initiatives. Leaving now means starting over with significant barriers to entry.
But if you’re beyond $10M-$15M in revenue, you know if it’s time to go.

Dear SaaStr: Is It Bad To Leave a Start-Up That's Not Going Very Well?
It’s not always bad. But if you leave too early, your career often suffers.
First, think about why you want to leave:
Are you burnt out from working long hours with no end in sight?
Do you feel undervalued or overworked without adequate compensation?
Is there no clear path for growth or advancement within the company?
If these are your reasons, it might be time to move on. Staying at a struggling startup can take a toll on both your mental and physical health. You deserve better.
But ask yourself one more question before making any decisions:

What do I need to learn here that will help me succeed elsewhere?
If you’re leaving because you don’t see success ahead, but you haven’t learned everything you could, you might regret it later.

A few things to consider:

How many startups have you worked at?
Have you experienced the full cycle—from idea generation through scale-up and IPO (if possible)?
Can you point to specific lessons—whether they were successes or failures—that helped shape who you are as an entrepreneur today?

Most importantly: what skills would you bring to your next role that you wouldn't otherwise have gained by staying through this challenging period?
Sometimes the best learning comes from experiencing failure firsthand. The companies we remember most aren't those that succeeded immediately; they're those that pushed through adversity to become something remarkable.

So while leaving may seem like the easy way out, it isn't always the right choice. Sometimes the hardest choices are the ones where you stay, fight, and learn.
And maybe … maybe find a new CEO.
I joined a start-up when it had just $20k MRR growing slowly. It was tough, but we got to $2m ARR growing 100% YoY. Then the cofounder left to go back to his old job. I tried to carry it further, but ultimately couldn't make it work.
Yes, I'd made some mistakes, and our customers didn't love us enough, etc. But I've never looked back and said I should have quit sooner. In fact, I wish I'd hired someone to help run it instead!
In contrast, my second start-up took off faster than expected. We hit $1M ARR in less than 12 months. And then... we lost almost all our leads overnight due to a big change in how Google works. So far, so good — we went down from $200k+ MRR to $0 overnight. Still, still doing fine. We're at $500k-$600k MRR now.

Your product needs serious maturation
Prospects want proof points before committing
You’re still refining your go-to-market motion
Customer success stories take months, not weeks, to develop

Month 1–3: Reps struggle because the product isn’t reliable or scalable. They lose credibility with prospects who hear contradictory things about capabilities.

We’ve talked on SaaStr many times how to manage cash.  But one thing I haven’t done enough is talk about how to avoid running out.
Yes, you can run a model and see when your runway ends. And maybe even build a zero-cash plan for next year.  But what if … you just don’t have time?  What if it’s too late?
Let me share my learnings here:
First,
never let your burn rate exceed twice your monthly revenue
.  This isn’t a rule per se, but it works well for most startups that raise some VC capital at least.  If you’re burning more than twice your last month’s MRR / ARR — then something has gone wrong.  You aren’t growing fast enough.  The sales team isn’t performing well enough.  Your CTO doesn’t know how to scale the product.  Something.
Because that means you’ll be running out of money in less than a year.
Second,
if you are worried you might run out of money before Year Two or so, never spend anything without talking to your co-founder first
.  Even if they don’t want to hear it.
In fact, make sure this is part of any investment round pitch deck discussion.  It should always come up.  “If we do worse than X, our cash will run out.”  Or “we expect $Xm ARR by Y months after funding.”

Don’t hire anyone with no equity until you have real traction.
Do not hire an unaffordable VP.
Never take a bonus or salary increase unless you have plenty of cash.
Never add another layer of management unless you really have the cash to pay them all.

But there are things you can do to save money each month, every month.  If you start now, you won’t ever get close to running out of money again.  At least, not from overspending.
